lens: who pays for the growth, and who has to sell stock
opinion: I think the names that bounced pay their own way, and most of the names that stayed down need other people's money. Of the ten that fell hard and came back, 10 of 10 earn a profit and 0 of 10 have new shares coming to market. Of the fifteen that stayed down, 4 of 15 earn a profit, 9 of 15 have new shares coming, and 13 of 15 grew their share count more than 3% in a year. In the run, the Nasdaq-100 fund rose while the average stock fell. My reading: buyers crowded into a few big profitable names, so a company with shares to sell had to take a lower price. But raised forecasts, from management and from analysts, split the groups more cleanly than funding does, and most weak names have both problems, so the file cannot tell me which did the damage. The leaders are now worth $7,710.58 billion, up from $6,594.93 billion on 15 September. The laggards went from $1,169.63 billion to $1,070.17 billion.

cbrs: CBRS had the growth the leaders had: its line shows guidance raised, the earnings estimate up 32.3% over 90 days, sales up 74.3% last quarter and its comps' median up 18.9% over the last month, yet the stock is down 4.7% over the month and -1.3% in the run. What it has that AMD, MRVL and TSM do not is supply and no earnings: it listed on 14 May 2026, about 171M of roughly 238M shares are coming out of lock-up (the period when early holders are barred from selling) in stages, with about 36.4M on 12 Aug and the last on 9 Nov, executives have been selling in size, and its share count is up 61.2% in a year against 1.1%, 2.6% and 0.0% for the other three, on top of spending more cash than it brings in (-$0.68 billion), no expected earnings to price it on, a price of 52.3 times sales against a comps median of 9.2, and three customers making 76% of sales. It is not short of money ($6.43 billion more cash than debt, nothing raised since 1 July), so this is early holders selling into every rally, not the company needing funds; a buyer of the chip bounce could own AMD, MRVL or TSM, which earn real profits, without standing in front of that selling.
weakest_point: The file's cleanest split is not funding. It is forecasts. Among the names that fell hard, management raised guidance at 10 of 10 that bounced and 1 of 14 that did not, and analysts cut earnings estimates at 0 of 10 against 10 of 11. That is a wider gap than share count (1 of 10 against 13 of 15) or new shares coming (0 of 10 against 9 of 15). Funding also fails on both sides. APP, BKNG, NFLX and IBM all earn a profit and bring in more cash than they spend (free cash flow $4.53, $9.54, $11.15 and $13.79 billion), and they are still in the bottom 20. Leaders sold paper and still led: NET priced $2.175B of convertible notes on 11 Aug, SMCI has free cash flow of -6.97 and share count up 11.0%, and AXTI's share count is up 40.1%. NBIS priced $5.0B of convertibles on 19 Aug and still ranks 38 of 145. Buying back stock shows 'no real difference' (leaders 12 of 24, laggards 7 of 22). So the market did take new shares when the numbers were going up. The file also has no data on who was buying or selling, so my 'narrow market starves the share-sellers' story is an inference, not something measured.
what_would_change_my_mind: If CBRS is still not moving a few weeks after its last lock-up release on 9 Nov while its comps keep rising, then supply was not the reason and I would drop this.
one_sentence: The stocks that bounced earn their own money and have no new shares coming, the ones that stayed down burn cash and keep feeding new shares into a market that is only buying the big profitable names, and CBRS is the clearest case because its numbers went up and its stock still did not.

opinion: I think your growth rule holds, but be exact about which growth. The size of next year's forecast did not separate these names. 14 of 17 laggards are expected to grow sales 15% or more next year, against 11 of 16 leaders. The biggest forecasts in the file belong to laggards: SHAZ 1195.1%, SMR 439.7%, CIFR 290.6%. What separated them was the direction the numbers were moving. Management raised its own forecast (guidance) at 24 of 25 leaders and 3 of 20 laggards. Analysts cut earnings estimates at 12 of 17 laggards and 2 of 23 leaders. Among names that fell hard, 10 of 10 that bounced had estimates raised; 10 of 11 that did not had them cut. Growth already delivered mattered less: 22 of 25 leaders grew sales 20% or more last quarter, but so did 9 of 21 laggards. Rising numbers were not enough alone. WDC and CBRS had them and still lagged. The leaders were picked on price, so this shows what went with the bounce, not what caused it.

evidence.claim: The size of next year's forecast did not separate them. The file's verdict on both the sales forecast and the earnings forecast is 'no real difference', and on sales the laggards score higher. Only 16 of the 25 leaders have a sales reading, so this line is thin on the leader side.

cbrs: CBRS is the one name my lens does not explain: its growth and its numbers looked like a leader's (sales up 74.3% last quarter, 232.7% forecast for next year, earnings estimate up 32.3% in 90 days, guidance raised), and its comps' median rose 24.1% in the run while CBRS fell 1.3%. What differed from AMD, MRVL and TSM sits around the growth, not in it: CBRS loses money (operating margin -265.0% against -55.3% a year ago, and no forward P/E to price it on), is priced at 52.3 times sales against a comps' median of 9.2, got 76% of its sales from its top three customers, and missed on headline sales at its last report ($180.1M against about $194M expected). Above all, its share count is up 61.2% in a year (AMD 1.1%, MRVL 2.6%, TSM 0.0%) and early lock-up releases (insiders' shares becoming free to sell after the May IPO) cover about 171M of roughly 238M shares, the last on 9 Nov, so I read it as numbers going up while a wave of stock for sale held the price down.
weakest_point: Rising numbers did not guarantee anything. WDC had guidance raised, its earnings estimate up 24.9%, sales up 43.8% last quarter and a forward P/E of 22.0 against a comps' median of 32.4, and it is still down 17.0% over three months at rank 126 of 145. MU (estimate up 26.3%, rank 57) and STX (estimate up 30.3%, rank 75) sat mid-field, and CBRS had the same upgrades and did not bounce. On the other side, META and S are leaders whose earnings estimates were cut. Also, "its comps' median is also up over the last month" separates the two sets nearly as well as guidance does (23 of 25 leaders against 3 of 22 laggards), so part of what I credit to revisions may simply be which group a stock sat in. And because leaders were picked on price and the file does not date the upgrades against the bounce, it cannot show which came first.
what_would_change_my_mind: If properly dated estimates showed the upgrades arrived after the 15 Sep bounce instead of before it, or if CBRS still does not recover after its last lock-up release on 9 Nov while its numbers keep rising, I would stop treating revisions as the driver.
one_sentence: The names that bounced were not the ones with the biggest growth forecasts, they were the ones whose numbers were being raised and who already earn money, while the laggards had bigger forecasts and falling estimates, and CBRS had rising numbers but no profits and a flood of new shares.

opinion:
I think the fundamentals here are mostly labels on where the money went. The leaders are two trades. 13 of 25 never fell: mainly security, software and storage names that rose all summer. Ten fell and bounced; all but DDOG are chip-industry names that came back when the chip fund did. In both, the whole business line moved: comps were up for 23 of 25 leaders against 3 of 22 laggards. Most laggards are miners, power and consumer internet names. Big beat small. And "raised estimates" is measured over the same 90 days as the price gain, so it describes the move as much as explains it.

But falling hard was not enough. Among names that all fell hard, 10 of 10 that bounced had raised guidance, against 1 of 14 that did not. So money picked the groups and rising forecasts picked the names inside them. For a buyer today, 19 of 25 leaders are priced above their comps on forward earnings, and those comps have already run. The good news is paid for.

evidence.claim: Whole business lines moved together, so a leader's comps mostly did what the leader did.
evidence.count: "its comps' median is also up over the last month": leaders 23 of 25, laggards 3 of 22; never-fell leaders 12 of 13. Cybersecurity cohort: 7 names, leaders CRWD, OKTA, S, PANW, NET, FTNT. Neoclouds & AI miners (12 names) and AI Powertrain (12 names): leaders none.

evidence.claim: Big beat small, and a few giants carry the leaders' dollar total (this also answers the market cap question).
evidence.count: "worth $25 billion or more": leaders 21 of 25, laggards 8 of 22. Leaders' market value $6,594.93B on 15 Sep to $7,710.58B now; laggards $1,169.63B to $1,070.17B. TSM $2,501.4B, META $1,880B, AMD $1,060B now.

evidence.claim: The same good news got opposite price reactions depending on the group's mood, so the raise did not set the timing.
evidence.count: On their raises CRWD 'jumped 20.5% the next day' and TWLO went 'up 25% in a day'; AMD 'fell 7% the next day' and DDOG 'fell 19% on 6 Aug after its Q2 report despite a beat and a raised guide'. Chip fund: -17.3 in the fall, 16.9 in the run, still -3.4 against 30 Jun.

evidence.claim: 'What fell hardest bounced hardest' covers only the chip half of the leaders, and as a rule it fails: the hardest-hit names are mostly laggards.
evidence.count: "ROSE between 30 June and 15 September while the chip fund fell 17%": leaders 13 of 25. "was down 30% or more at its worst": leaders 5 of 25, laggards 11 of 22. Whole field: 34 'fell hard, then bounced hard', 22 'fell hard and did not bounce'.

evidence.claim: Among names that all fell hard, the direction of forecasts marked who came back. The group marked it almost as well.
evidence.count: Raised guidance: bounced 10 of 10, did not 1 of 14. Analysts cut the earnings estimate: 0 of 10 against 10 of 11. Comps' median also up: 9 of 10 against 2 of 15.

evidence.claim: Expected growth and raised forecasts on their own do not pick the winners.
evidence.count: "sales expected to grow 15% or more next fiscal year": leaders 11 of 16, laggards 14 of 17 ('no real difference'). MU, SNDK, STX and WDC all show guidance 'raised' and earnings estimate 'up', yet rank 57, 80, 75 and 126 of 145.

evidence.claim: Most leaders are priced above their comps, and those comps have already risen. The exceptions are named.
evidence.count: "forward P/E is ABOVE its comps' median": leaders 19 of 25 (the ten that bounced: 9 of 10, and EV/sales above comps 10 of 10). Not above: NTAP, TSM, SMCI, NTNX, ADI, META. Examples: CRWD 193.3 vs 50.3, NET 240.2 vs 50.3, DDOG 104.8 vs 21.2.

cbrs: CBRS had the same good news as AMD, MRVL and TSM: guidance raised, the earnings estimate up 32.3% in 90 days, sales up 74.3% last quarter, and comps whose median rose 24.1 in the run. It still lost 1.3 in the run because a wave of stock is for sale: early lock-up releases (early holders becoming free to sell) cover about 171M of roughly 238M shares in fortnightly steps, the last on 9 Nov, executives are selling, and the share count is up 61.2% in a year against 1.1, 2.6 and 0.0 for AMD, MRVL and TSM. It also loses money (operating margin -265.0, no forward P/E to price it on) and already sits at 52.3 times sales against 9.2 for its comps, so the money coming back to chips had profitable names to buy and no shortage of CBRS sellers.
weakest_point: The both-fell-hard cut argues against me. Fifteen names fell as hard as the ten that bounced and did not come back, so falling was not the cause. Raised guidance splits them 10 of 10 against 1 of 14, and analysts cut the earnings estimate for 0 of 10 against 10 of 11. For those ten the raise also came first: AMD 'fell 7% the next day' and DDOG 'fell 19%' on their reports, and the bounce came weeks later. So there the raise is not the price move relabelled. It came before the move and it marked who recovered. Two leaders, DDOG and META, also rose while their own comps' medians were down 7.4 and 4.4 over the month. My one reply: the did-not list is nearly all miners, nuclear and power names, so that cut cannot fully separate 'raised guidance' from 'is a chip name'.
what_would_change_my_mind: I would change my mind if, inside a single group that rose, the names that raised guidance clearly beat the names that did not; the file has fundamentals for only 52 of the 145 names, so it cannot show that yet.
one_sentence: Money moved into big, profitable groups (security software that never fell, chips that fell and came back), rising forecasts decided which names inside those groups got lifted, and 19 of 25 leaders are now priced above comps that have already run.

cbrs_explanations.explanation: 1. Analysts cut its numbers. No. Analysts raised them. CBRS is one of only three laggards with a higher earnings estimate and one of two with a higher sales estimate. Two cautions. The sales reading rests on a single read, not two that agree. And the file gives no forward P/E (price against next year's expected earnings) for CBRS, so it does not show whether the higher estimate is a profit or just a smaller loss.
cbrs_explanations.evidence: CBRS line: eps_estimate_90d "up", eps_estimate_90d_pct 32.3, eps_estimate_status "two readings agree"; sales_estimate_90d "up"; forward_pe null. Counts: analysts RAISED the earnings estimate, leaders "21 of 23", laggards "3 of 17" (APLD, WDC, CBRS). Analysts CUT the earnings estimate, laggards "12 of 17", CBRS not on that list. Analysts RAISED the sales estimate, laggards "2 of 7" (WDC, CBRS), but where two readings agree "laggards 0 of 2". Among names that fell hard: raised earnings estimate, bounced "10 of 10", did not "1 of 11". By elimination that one is CBRS (APLD and WDC are classed "in between").

cbrs_explanations.explanation: 2. Management lowered guidance. No. Management raised it at the 12 Aug report and both readings agree. The three laggards that lowered guidance are IBM, OKLO and EOSE.
cbrs_explanations.evidence: CBRS line: guidance "raised", guidance_status "two readings agree"; last_report: "core" revenue of $209.9M (+103%) "beat the company's own ~$194M guide". Counts: management RAISED guidance, leaders "24 of 25", laggards "3 of 20" (RDDT, WDC, CBRS). Management LOWERED guidance, leaders "0 of 25", laggards "3 of 20" (IBM, OKLO, EOSE). Among names that fell hard: raised guidance, bounced "10 of 10", did not "1 of 14". By elimination that one is CBRS.

cbrs_explanations.explanation: 3. It loses money and the losses are widening. Yes on the reported figures. CBRS is not profitable and its operating loss is far larger against sales than a year ago. AMD, MRVL and TSM all earn a profit with margins up. Three leaders also lose money (LITE, S, NET), but each has a margin that improved, so it is the direction that sets CBRS apart. One caution: the file's account blames a "heavy stock-comp loss" (staff paid in shares after the May listing) and does not say how much of the loss that is. So the file cannot tell you whether the underlying business loss is widening.
cbrs_explanations.evidence: CBRS: profitable false; operating_margin_now_and_year_ago_pct [-265.0, -55.3]; story: "a GAAP revenue miss and heavy stock-comp loss on 12 Aug knocked it 14-17%". Cohort mates, same field: AMD [17.2, -1.7], MRVL [16.7, 14.9], TSM [60.3, 49.6], all profitable true. Loss-making leaders: LITE [27.9, -0.7], S [-22.7, -31.7], NET [-7.6, -12.4]. Counts among names that fell hard: earns a profit, bounced "10 of 10", did not "4 of 15"; operating margin higher than a year ago, bounced "10 of 10", did not "5 of 14".

cbrs_explanations.explanation: 4. It burns cash and needs outside money. Half right, and the half that matters is wrong. It does spend more cash than it brings in. But it holds far more cash than debt and has raised no money since 1 July. The file shows no funding need. The new stock reaching the market is locked-up shares being freed and executives selling, which the file records separately from the company raising money.
cbrs_explanations.evidence: CBRS: fcf_12m_b -0.68 (cash out exceeded cash in by $0.68 billion over twelve months); cash_less_debt_b 6.43; raised_money_since_1jul false; buying_back false. Cohort mates fcf_12m_b: AMD 8.4, MRVL 1.73, TSM 35.97. Counts: holds more cash than debt, laggards "8 of 22" with CBRS on the yes list; raised money since 1 July, laggards "9 of 21" with CBRS not on the list; brings in more cash than it spends, among names that fell hard, bounced "9 of 10", did not "4 of 15".

cbrs_explanations.explanation: 5. Its share count is rising and locked-up shares are being released. Yes. This is the best fit in the file, and no leader's line shows a lock-up. CBRS listed on 14 May and insiders' shares are being unlocked in stages, with the last release still to come on 9 Nov, alongside large executive sales. Its three cohort mates have almost no share growth and no new shares coming. Two cautions. A higher share count alone is not the reason: AXTI, a leader, has share count up 40.1% and bounced 50.2%. What is different at CBRS is supply that is still arriving. And the file shows the timing fits; it does not prove the releases caused the fall. The "story" is a written account, not a test.
cbrs_explanations.evidence: CBRS: share_count_1y_pct 61.2; new_shares_coming true; events: "IPO 14 May 2026 at $185. Staggered early lock-up release, 11 dates in all, about 171M shares in the first 10 of roughly 238M outstanding"; "In the window: 12 Aug 2026 about 36.4M shares"; story: "fortnightly early lock-up releases (about 171M shares, the last on 9 Nov), large executive sales". Cohort mates share_count_1y_pct: AMD 1.1, MRVL 2.6, TSM 0.0; new_shares_coming false for all three. AXTI: share_count_1y_pct 40.1, run_15sep_pct 50.2, new_shares_coming false. Counts among names that fell hard: share count up more than 3%, bounced "1 of 10", did not "13 of 15"; new shares hit or are about to hit the market, bounced "0 of 10", did not "9 of 15".

cbrs_explanations.explanation: 6. Its sales lean on a few customers. True of CBRS, but weak as the reason. Three customers are 76% of its sales. Yet MRVL, a leader in the same cohort, books 37% of sales through one distributor and bounced 22.4%. The file itself rates this gap "leans", not "clear". The CBRS account starts to mention news about an OpenAI workload and is cut off mid-word. So the file cannot tell you what that news was or how much it hurt.
cbrs_explanations.evidence: CBRS: customers "high"; top_customer_pct 34; customers_words: "Customer A 34% of revenue, Customer B 32%, Customer C 10% (top three 76%). Six months to 30 Jun 2026: Customer A 49%"; story ends "news that an OpenAI workloa". MRVL: customers "high", top_customer_pct 37, "Distributor A 37% of net revenue", run_15sep_pct 22.4. AMD customers "low"; TSM "moderate", top_customer_pct 19. Counts: leans on a few customers, leaders "7 of 24", laggards "10 of 18", how_sure "leans"; among names that fell hard, bounced "3 of 10", did not "9 of 12".

cbrs_explanations.explanation: 7. It is priced far above its comps. True as a fact, but the study's own counts say this does not separate winners from losers. CBRS is priced at 52.3 times sales against 9.2 for its comps. But being dearer than comps on that measure is as common among leaders as laggards, and all ten names that bounced are dearer than their comps. CRWD is priced at the same 52.3 times sales and ranks 3 of 145. So a high price alone did not hold a stock back. My reading, not the file's: a high price with no profit behind it leaves less room for bad news. The file has no forward P/E for CBRS to test that.
cbrs_explanations.evidence: CBRS: ev_sales 52.3, comps_median_ev_sales 9.2; forward_pe null, comps_median_forward_pe 29.1. Cohort mates ev_sales against comps: AMD 25.5 against 17.6, MRVL 27.2 against 17.6, TSM 17.0 against 15.9. CRWD (rank 3): ev_sales 52.3 against 10.4. NET (rank 13): 50.2 against 10.4. Counts: EV/sales above comps' median, leaders "18 of 25", laggards "17 of 22", how_sure "no real difference"; among names that fell hard, bounced "10 of 10", did not "12 of 15". Has forward earnings to be priced on: leaders "25 of 25", laggards "11 of 22", CBRS not on the yes list.

cbrs_explanations.explanation: 8. Its comps did not bounce either. No. Its comps rose strongly while it fell. That rules out the excuse that its whole corner of the market was weak. It also means CBRS sits on the leaders' side of the study's second-biggest gap and still did not bounce. One thing to know: over three months CBRS is up 2.8%, the same as its cohort's middle figure, so the gap opened in the last month. The 3-month count (63 sessions) starts later than 30 Jun, which is why CBRS can be up 2.8% over three months and down 16.7% in the fall.
cbrs_explanations.evidence: CBRS: comps_median_ret_1m_pct 18.9; comps_median_run_pct 24.1; own ret_1m_pct -4.7; run_15sep_pct -1.3; ret_3m_pct 2.8; fall_30jun_15sep_pct -16.7. Cohort AI ACCELERATORS & LOGIC (13 names): median_run_pct 18.1, median_1m_pct 19.8, median_3m_pct 2.8. run_15sep_pct: AMD 25.3, MRVL 22.4, TSM 17.4. Counts: its comps' median is also up over the last month, leaders "23 of 25", laggards "3 of 22" (IBM, WDC, CBRS); among names that fell hard, bounced "9 of 10", did not "2 of 15".

cbrs_explanations.explanation: 9. The business is slowing. No, on what the file has. Sales grew faster last quarter than at AMD, MRVL or TSM, analysts expect faster growth next year, and management raised guidance. The headline sales figure missed what analysts expected, but the file puts that down to how warrants given to OpenAI are booked, and the "core" figure beat. Two loose ends. The file has no earlier quarters, so it cannot show a trend directly. And the cut-off OpenAI workload news could be a demand worry the file does not spell out. Also note that expected sales growth does not separate leaders from laggards in this study at all.
cbrs_explanations.evidence: CBRS: sales_growth_last_q_pct 74.3; sales_growth_next_fy_pct 232.7; guidance "raised"; last_report: "GAAP revenue $180.1M (+74%) missed ~$194M consensus because of OpenAI warrant accounting, while \"core\" revenue of $209.9M (+103%) beat the company's own ~$194M guide". Cohort mates sales_growth_last_q_pct: AMD 50.1, MRVL 36.5, TSM 36.0. Counts: sales grew 20% or more in the latest quarter, leaders "22 of 25", laggards "9 of 21" with CBRS on the yes list; sales expected to grow 15% or more next fiscal year, leaders "11 of 16", laggards "14 of 17", how_sure "no real difference".

cbrs_answer: CBRS breaks the study's main rule: analysts raised its earnings estimate (up 32.3%), management raised guidance, sales grew 74.3% and its comps rose 18.9% in the last month, yet it fell 1.3% in the run while AMD, MRVL and TSM rose 25.3%, 22.4% and 17.4%. What sets it apart in the file is stock supply and losses: about 171M of roughly 238M shares are being unlocked after its 14 May listing (the last release is 9 Nov) with large executive sales, it loses money (operating margin -265.0% against -55.3% a year ago), it is priced at 52.3 times sales against 9.2 for its comps, and three customers are 76% of sales. It is not short of cash: it holds $6.43 billion more cash than debt and has raised no money since 1 July. The file cannot prove which of these held the stock down, because it is one stock, each trait except the lock-up also shows up in at least one leader, the written account is cut off mid-word at news about an OpenAI workload, and CBRS ranks 112 of 145, which is lower-middle rather than one of the 20 worst.

named.line: Rank 76 of 145, mid-field, not a laggard. Sales grew 112.5% and guidance was raised, but it owes $46.03 billion more than it holds in cash, spent $13.66 billion more than it took in over twelve months, and sold a $3.7B convertible (debt that can turn into shares) in September. It fell 18.7% in the fall and got back 8.0% in the run.

Rank 104 of 145, lower-middle; it is in the laggard set because it was named, not because it is one of the 20 worst. Unlike CBRS, its numbers are getting worse: sales fell 26.7% last quarter and the earnings estimate was cut, while share count is up 41.6% and it spent $2.23 billion more than it took in. Its comps fell too (-4.2% over the month).

Rank 38 of 145, upper-middle and the best of these seven, but outside the top 25. Sales grew 454.0% and it rose 12.2% in the run against 3.0% for its comps. What keeps it out of the leaders: the earnings estimate was cut (down 29.7%), guidance was only maintained, and it sold $5.0B of convertible notes in August with share count up 22.1%. (The file marks it profitable yet shows a GAAP operating loss of $175.9M, so treat that flag with care.)

Rank 57 of 145, mid-field. The business reads like a leader's (sales up 379.3%, earnings estimate up 26.3%, guidance raised), but the stock got back 14.7% in the run against 21.4% for its comps after falling 19.6%. It is priced at 6.0 times next year's expected earnings against 34.9 for comps, with sales expected to grow 14.4% next year; the file does not say why, but that price looks like doubt that the memory boom lasts.

Rank 80 of 145, mid-field. It fell 32.7% in the fall and got back 11.3%, even though sales grew 371.6%, the earnings estimate rose 13.9% and guidance was raised. The file's account is a price story, not a business one: it had run to "about $2,088 on 1 Jul" and was hit by "a sharp memory-sector shakeout in July".

Rank 75 of 145, mid-field. Earnings estimate up 30.3%, guidance raised, and it rose 14.9% in the run against 9.6% for its comps. That only partly repaired a 20.0% fall, so its 3-month return is 7.2% and its trend reading is still negative (-0.15).

Rank 126 of 145, the only one of the seven inside the 20 worst, and the best-placed of those 20. It is there on price alone: down 35.5% in the fall, back 7.2% in the run, 3-month return -17.0%. The business looks like a leader's (sales up 43.8%, earnings estimate up 24.9%, guidance raised, comps up 8.6% over the month). The file's only reason is that the stock "had run hard into the 5 Aug report, sold off 13% on a beat-and-raise and kept sliding"; a second hit in early October is cut off in the text.

must_say: How the groups were picked. Leaders and laggards were chosen by price alone: 3-month return, 1-month return and a trend score (the 'Hub Geiger', which the file does not explain), ranked across 145 names. Top 25 = leaders, bottom 20 = laggards. So 'the leaders went up' is how they were chosen, not something the study found. The 1-month window also covers the run itself.

CBRS and IREN were added to the laggards by hand. On the study's own ranking they are mid-field: CBRS is rank 112 of 145 and IREN rank 104 of 145, and both are slightly up over three months (2.8 and 1.7). CBRS is also the exception to the main finding: guidance raised, earnings estimate up 32.3, sales estimate up, and its comps' median up 18.9 over the month. What CBRS shares with the laggards is share supply: share count up 61.2 on a year, insiders' shares coming free to sell (lock-up releases of about 171M of roughly 238M shares), no profit, and three customers at 76% of revenue. The headline finding does not explain CBRS; the share-supply finding does.

Only the extremes were read. 52 of the 145 names were studied: the 25 leaders, the 22 laggards and five mid-field names. The middle of the field was not read. The study shows how the best differ from the worst. It cannot show how the best differ from an average name.

The mid-field names that were read weaken the story. MU, SNDK and STX all have raised guidance, higher earnings estimates, profits and positive cash flow, yet rank 57, 80 and 75 of 145. WDC has all of that and is a laggard at rank 126. So the leader profile is something leaders share, not a guarantee.

Much of the gap is which group a stock sits in. 'Its comps' median is also up over the last month' separates the groups nearly as well as anything about the company itself: 23 of 25 leaders against 3 of 22 laggards. CRWD, OKTA, S, PANW, NET and FTNT are leaders out of a cybersecurity cohort of 7 names. The neocloud / miner cohort supplies WULF, CIFR, APLD, CORZ, RIOT and IREN to the laggards; the power cohort supplies SMR, NRG, UUUU, OKLO, EOSE and LEU. The study has not separated 'good company' from 'right group'.

Half the leaders did not bounce at all. Only 10 of the 25 'fell hard, then bounced hard'. 13 of 25 leaders rose between 30 June and 15 September while the chip fund fell 17%; these are mostly cybersecurity and software, and in that same stretch the software fund rose 16.5 and the cybersecurity fund 12.4. LITE and ADI are 'in between'. Of the ten that bounced (AMD, AXTI, ENTG, MRVL, TER, FORM, TSM, TSEM, MPWR, DDOG), all but DDOG are chip, chip-equipment or chip-materials names, and the chip fund itself rose 16.9 in the run.

The bounce comparison is small and hand-picked by result. Across the whole field 34 names 'fell hard, then bounced hard'; the study read only the 10 that are leaders, which are the strongest of them. 22 'fell hard and did not bounce'; the study read 15. So the '10 of 10' lines are 10 names against 15 or fewer.

What 'raised estimates' can and cannot prove. The estimate readings cover 'the last 90 days', read on 6 Oct. That is the same three months used to rank the stocks. A good report lifts the stock and lifts analysts' numbers together, and analysts also raise numbers after a stock has run. The file shows the two went together. It cannot show which came first, and it contains no test where the estimate was read before the price move. The fairest evidence is inside the bounce group, where the good report came first and the stock fell anyway before running after 15 September (TSM reported 16 Jul, TSEM 4-5 Aug, DDOG 6 Aug). That is real, but it is 10 names, nearly all chips.

'Raised' is a direction, not a size. It puts OKTA at 2.3 and TWLO at 2.4 in the same box as SMCI at 43.7 and P at 40.2. For AXTI, ENTG, NTAP, FORM, TSM and MPWR the size is blank. The file does not say which fiscal year each estimate refers to. For loss-making names the percentages are meaningless (IREN -1890, WULF -220).

'Raised guidance' means raised versus not raised, not raised versus cut. Only 3 of 20 laggards lowered guidance (IBM, OKLO, EOSE), and the file marks that gap 'leans'. SHAZ, CIFR, SMR, APLD, CORZ and RIOT give no guidance at all and are counted as 'not raised'. APP and BKNG were left out because the two readings disagreed.

Several lines are thin and should be labelled as hints. Sales estimates: only 7 laggards have a reading ('2 of 7' raised, '3 of 7' cut) and the two independent readings agree on just 2 of them ('0 of 2'); in the bounce cut it is '1 of 4' and '3 of 4'. Across all 52 names the two readings agree on sales-estimate direction for 18, 15 rest on a single reading and 19 have none. Earnings-estimate direction is unknown for CRWD, PANW, CIFR, EOSE, RIOT, LEU and RDDT, so laggards are counted out of 17. Price against expected earnings versus comps (forward P/E) rests on 11 laggards. Next-year earnings growth rests on 9 laggards; next-year sales growth on 16 leaders.

Where the figures came from. Business figures are public web pages read on 6 Oct by one reader per company and re-checked by a second; estimate direction and guidance were also read blind by a third. The live database was not read. The checker changed something on all 52 names, 432 changes in total, so the first pass was not clean. Only 23 names were cross-checked against the Hub, and not all matched: forward P/E within 25% on 15 of 17, EV/sales within 25% on 19 of 23, next-year sales growth within 8 points on 14 of 17. Price data showed no mismatches. Small slips are visible in the text (AXTI's note gives a window ending '6 Dec 2026').

The comps are not listed. The file gives each name's comps' median but not who the comps are or how they were chosen, and it says the live database was not read. Alan asked for the comps system's comparables, so the page must say whether these are that system's lists. Some look odd: IBM (forward P/E 17.4) is set against comps with a median forward P/E of 50.6. 135 peers were read; 119 had a forward P/E.

Growth: the file backs half of Alan's rule. Growth already delivered separates the groups ('sales grew 20% or more in the latest quarter': 22 of 25 leaders, 9 of 21 laggards). Growth forecast does not: 'sales expected to grow 15% or more next fiscal year' is 11 of 16 leaders against 14 of 17 laggards, marked 'no real difference', and it leans the wrong way. Some laggards have the fastest sales growth in the study off tiny bases and no profit (SHAZ 412.3, UUUU 496.1, APLD 406.6, EOSE 351.4). The winners are growth that already earns money, not growth that is promised.

The leaders are not cheap. Company value against sales versus comps (EV/sales) shows 'no real difference': 18 of 25 leaders and 17 of 22 laggards are above their comps' median. On forward P/E the leaders are the dearer ones: 19 of 25 trade above their comps' median (marked 'leans').

The list of conditions is not a list of separate proofs. 'Earns a profit', 'free cash flow above zero', 'has a forward P/E', 'share count up more than 3%', 'new shares coming' and 'raised money' mostly describe the same loss-making miner and nuclear names. Among the laggards that do earn a profit (APP, BKNG, NFLX, NRG, IBM, LEU, RDDT, WDC) only NRG, LEU and WDC are on the share-count-up list. 'Earns a profit' is also bent by one-offs: LITE is marked not profitable with an operating margin of 27.9.

Market value, with the concentration stated. In $ billion: leaders 6594.93 on 15 Sep to 7710.58 at the last close on file (5 Oct); laggards 1169.63 to 1070.17; the whole field of 145 from 38893.20 to 41932.86. The leader total is dominated by three names: TSM at 2501.4, META at 1880 and AMD at 1060. Four leaders are under $25 billion (S, AXTI, FORM, NTNX). A total does not describe the typical leader.

Name the exceptions among the leaders. META is a leader with guidance 'maintained', its earnings estimate 'down' (-2.6), its comps' median down (-4.4) and a lower operating margin than a year ago. S had its earnings estimate cut (-6.1). NET and SMCI are leaders with new shares coming.
must_not_claim: Anything about what happens next. The file stops at the 5 Oct close. It has no test of whether leaders keep leading, laggards recover, or raised estimates keep paying.

That raised guidance or raised estimates CAUSED the bounce. The groups were picked by price after the fact and the estimate readings cover the same three months. The file shows they went together, nothing more.
That raised estimates are enough to pick a winner, or a rule to buy on. WDC, CBRS and APLD had earnings estimates raised and are laggards. MU, SNDK and STX had them raised and sit mid-field.
That the leaders are the faster growers looking ahead. Next-year sales growth of 15% or more is 11 of 16 leaders against 14 of 17 laggards, 'no real difference'.
That the leaders are cheap, or that valuation explains the gap. EV/sales shows 'no real difference', and 19 of 25 leaders trade above their comps on forward P/E.
That the leaders are 'overbought' or due a pullback. The file has no overbought measure, and the trend score it uses is not defined in it.

That these 25 names are what pushed the indexes higher. The file has no index weights. In the largest cohort, AI ACCELERATORS & LOGIC, value rose from 10988.2 to 12551.1, and its three leaders (AMD 822.8 to 1060, MRVL 194.4 to 251.9, TSM 2145.6 to 2501.4) account for less than half of that rise. Most of it came from names that are not on the leader list.
That CBRS is a typical laggard, or that falling estimates explain it. It is rank 112 of 145, its guidance was raised and its earnings estimate is up 32.3.
That the laggards are cutting guidance. Only 3 of 20 lowered it. Most kept it or give none.
That every leader 'bounced'. 13 of 25 never fell in the first place.

That buybacks, customer concentration or sales-estimate cuts are established findings. Buybacks are 'no real difference' (12 of 24 against 7 of 22). Customer concentration is 'leans' (7 of 24 against 10 of 18). Sales-estimate cuts rest on 7 laggards.
That the figures come from, or were verified against, the Scintilla database or comps system. The file says the live database was not read.
That this holds for the whole field or the whole market. 52 of 145 names were read, all from AI, chip, software and grid cohorts, over one three-month stretch.
That there are twenty-odd separate reasons. Many of the conditions describe the same companies.

extra_cuts.cut: Strip out the group move. For each of the 25 leaders and 22 laggards take `run_15sep_pct` minus `comps_median_run_pct` (and `ret_1m_pct` minus `comps_median_ret_1m_pct`). Split the 47 into 'beat its comps' and 'lagged its comps' and re-count the top conditions: `guidance` = raised, `eps_estimate_90d` = up, `profitable` = true, `share_count_1y_pct` above 3, `new_shares_coming` = true. As a spot check, compare the same fields inside the five cohorts listed under SAME COHORT, DIFFERENT OUTCOME (for example P and NTAP against WDC, MU, SNDK and STX).
extra_cuts.why: It tells you whether the fundamentals explain the stock or only the sector. If the gaps shrink, the finding is really 'chips and cybersecurity went up, miners and nuclear went down'. A first look says they will shrink: in Memory & Storage all six names have guidance raised and earnings estimates up, and in Internet the leader META has guidance 'maintained' and its estimate 'down' while the laggard RDDT 'raised'. ADI (16.0 against comps 24.2) and TSM (17.4 against 21.4) are leaders that trailed their own comps in the run.

extra_cuts.cut: The 'ticks every box' test. Across all 52 studied names (leaders, laggards and the five named mid-field), list every name with `guidance` = raised AND `eps_estimate_90d` = up AND `profitable` = true AND `fcf_12m_b` above 0. Show each one's `rank`, `group` and `run_15sep_pct`. Then add `share_count_1y_pct` above 3 or `new_shares_coming` = true and see whether that explains the ones that did not lead.
extra_cuts.why: It tests whether the leader profile is enough to make a leader, or only what leaders have in common. The file already shows misses: WDC (rank 126), SNDK (rank 80), STX (rank 75) and MU (rank 57) tick all four. Share supply explains some of them (WDC share count up 6.7, STX 5.5) but not MU (1.6) or SNDK (0.4). If many box-tickers sit outside the leaders, the opinion has to say 'needed, but not enough'.

extra_cuts.cut: Size of the estimate change against size of the move. For every studied name with a number in `eps_estimate_90d_pct`, set it beside `run_15sep_pct` and `ret_3m_pct`, leaders and laggards shown separately. Leave out names where `profitable` is false, since the percentage means nothing there (IREN -1890, WULF -220, SHAZ -169.7).
extra_cuts.why: The headline uses direction only. If bigger raises went with bigger runs (P 40.2 and 48.4; TER 18.4 and 33.6) the estimate story gets stronger. If they did not (SMCI 43.7 and 21.2; TWLO 2.4 and 24.3; CBRS 32.3 and -1.3; WDC 24.9 and 7.2) it gets weaker. It also shows how many 'raised' leaders had only a small raise (OKTA 2.3, DDOG 3.9, NET 4.1, NTNX 4.3).

extra_cuts.cut: Who added the dollars. Per name, `cap_now_b` minus `cap_15sep_b` for the 25 leaders and the 22 laggards, ranked. Compare the leader total with the field's `now_b` minus `run_start_b` in MARKET VALUE, and with each cohort's `value_now_b` minus `value_15sep_b` in COHORTS. Give the median `cap_now_b` of each group next to the totals.
extra_cuts.why: It answers Alan's market-cap question properly and tests his premise that these names pushed the indexes up. The leader total (6594.93 to 7710.58) is dominated by TSM 2501.4, META 1880 and AMD 1060, while the whole field rose from 38893.20 to 41932.86, so much of the dollar gain may sit in names that are not leaders. A median shows the typical leader, which the total hides.

overall: As a description the main finding holds: the leaders are mostly profitable companies that raised guidance and are not issuing shares (24 of 25 raised guidance against 3 of 20 laggards), and the laggards are mostly loss-making miner and nuclear names that are issuing them. It is not solid as an explanation of why they bounced, because the groups were picked by price after the fact, the estimate readings cover the same three months, and the figures are web reads in which the checker changed something on all 52 names. The single most likely way it is wrong: it tells you what the losers lacked, not what made the winners win. The middle of the field was never read, the mid-field names that were read (MU, SNDK, STX) and the laggards WDC and CBRS had the same raised guidance and rising estimates without leading, and 'its comps are also up' (23 of 25 against 3 of 22) says much of the gap is simply which group a stock is in.

verdicts.condition: management RAISED its own guidance at the last report
verdicts.why: Guidance means management's own forecast. This is the best-supported line in the study: leaders 24 of 25, laggards 3 of 20. Where two readers agree it is leaders 23 of 24, laggards 3 of 19. On the harder cut it is 10 of 10 bouncers against 1 of 14 non-bouncers. For the names that fell then bounced, the raise was public before the run began (reports dated 16 Jul to 27 Aug), so a buyer could have known it. Three caveats. First, it sorts groups, not stocks inside a group. In the accelerator cohort CBRS raised just like AMD, MRVL and TSM. In memory WDC, MU, SNDK and STX raised just like P and NTAP. In internet the leader META only maintained and the laggard RDDT raised. The single non-bouncer that raised is CBRS, the only chip name in that set. Second, the harder cut is less hard than it looks: the bouncers are chip names plus DDOG, and the chip fund itself rose 16.9 in the run. Third, for the 13 that never fell, the raise was the price jump (CRWD up 20.5% the next day, TWLO up 25% in a day), so it could not be bought ahead. Also SHAZ, CIFR, SMR, APLD, CORZ and RIOT give no guidance at all, so 'did not raise' partly means 'is a miner or a pre-revenue builder'. A raise was close to required. It was never enough.

verdicts.condition: its comps' median is also up over the last month
verdicts.why: This is a group label by design. It asks whether the comparable companies went up, not anything about the company. Leaders 23 of 25, laggards 3 of 22, one reading only. Inside the accelerator cohort AMD, MRVL, TSM and the laggard CBRS all show the same peer figure, 18.9. In memory the peers of WDC (8.6), MU and SNDK (18.9) are up as much as those of leaders P and NTAP (7.5). In internet the leader META (-4.4) has falling peers just like the laggards. In software the leader DDOG (-7.4) has falling peers like the laggard APP (-6.3). It is also circular: last month's return is one of the three scores that define a leader, so 'your peers rose that same month' is the same tape. The harder cut (9 of 10 against 2 of 15) only says chips bounced and miners and power names did not.

verdicts.condition: analysts RAISED the earnings estimate over the last 90 days
verdicts.why: Leaders 21 of 23, laggards 3 of 17. Two readers agree on leaders 20 of 22, laggards 3 of 14. Harder cut: 10 of 10 against 1 of 11. But it is not a second finding. Analysts lift their numbers after management lifts its forecast, so this is the guidance line counted again. The 90 days are the same three months the price is measured over, and the file does not date the changes, so it cannot show the estimate moved before the price did. Same-cohort test: it splits servers (SMCI up, SHAZ down) and software (TWLO, NTNX, DDOG up; APP down). It does not split accelerators (CBRS up 32.3), memory (WDC up 24.9; MU, SNDK, STX up) or internet (leader META down 2.6). No usable reading for CRWD, PANW, CIFR, EOSE, RIOT, LEU, RDDT.

verdicts.condition: analysts RAISED the sales estimate over the last 90 days
verdicts.why: The laggard side is nearly empty. Laggards are 2 of 7, and where two readers agree it is 0 of 2. Across everything read, two readers agree on 18 names, 15 rest on one reader and 19 have no reading. The harder cut has 1 of 4 on the non-bounce side. The two laggards with a raise, WDC and CBRS, are the ones sitting next to leaders in chip cohorts, so inside chips it does not split at all. Probably true, and probably the same news as the guidance raise. Four to seven readings cannot carry a claim.

verdicts.condition: analysts CUT the earnings estimate over the last 90 days
verdicts.why: Mirror image of the raise line, so the same finding a third time. Leaders 2 of 23, laggards 12 of 17. Two readers agree on 2 of 22 against 10 of 14. Harder cut: 0 of 10 against 10 of 11. Weak points. For loss-makers the figure is a deeper loss, not a cut to earnings, and the sizes mean nothing (WULF -220, IREN -1890, SHAZ -169.7). DKNG and NRG rest on one reader. A cut did not decide the outcome: leader S was cut 6.1 and laggard NRG was cut 6.1; leader META was cut 2.6 and laggard IBM 2.3. For some laggards the cut and the fall were the same news on the same day (IBM fell 25.2% on its 14 Jul warning), so nobody could act on it first. Same-cohort test: it splits servers and software, not accelerators or memory (nobody was cut there, CBRS and WDC lagged anyway), and not internet (META was cut too).

verdicts.condition: earns a profit (earnings per share above zero over twelve months)
verdicts.why: Leaders 22 of 25, laggards 8 of 22, one reading. The loss-making laggards are mostly miners turned data-centre landlords (WULF, CIFR, APLD, CORZ, RIOT, IREN) and nuclear, uranium and battery names (SMR, UUUU, OKLO, EOSE). Those cohorts have no leader at all. Where a cohort holds both, profit does not sort them. APP has a 77.7 operating margin and is a laggard next to leader TWLO at 7.8. BKNG, NFLX, RDDT, IBM and WDC all earn a profit and lagged. LITE, S and NET lose money and lead. It splits only against CBRS and SHAZ, a new listing and a pre-revenue builder. The flag itself is shaky: LITE counts as loss-making with a 27.9 operating margin, CRWD counts as profitable at -2.3. The checker changed something on all 52 names read, 432 changes in all, and this figure had no third reader. The harder cut (10 of 10 against 4 of 15) passes only because the non-bouncers are those same miners and developers.

verdicts.condition: brings in more cash than it spends (free cash flow above zero)
verdicts.why: Leaders 23 of 25, laggards 9 of 22, one reading. Every laggard that burns cash is a miner, a power name, SHAZ or CBRS. Every laggard outside those groups brings in cash and lagged anyway: APP 4.53, BKNG 9.54, NFLX 11.15, IBM 13.79, WDC 3.51 (in $ billions). Same-cohort test: it splits only accelerators (CBRS -0.68). In servers the leader SMCI burns more (-6.97) than the laggard SHAZ (-0.31). In memory, software and internet everyone is cash-positive. Harder cut 9 of 10 against 4 of 15 reflects the same mix of company types.

verdicts.condition: has forward earnings to be priced on (a forward P/E exists)
verdicts.why: Leaders 25 of 25, laggards 11 of 22, one reading. This is the profit line again under another name: a company with no expected earnings has no price-to-earnings figure. The laggards without one are miners, power names, SHAZ and CBRS. Every laggard in internet, software, memory and IT services has one and still lagged, several of them cheap against their comparables (APP 15.7 against 30.0, BKNG 14.2 against 26.8, IBM 17.4 against 50.6). And 'has earnings to be priced on' is generous for leaders priced at 193.3 (CRWD) or 240.2 (NET) times. Harder cut 10 of 10 against 6 of 15: same mix.

verdicts.condition: operating margin is higher than a year ago
verdicts.why: Leaders 23 of 25, laggards 9 of 21, one reading. It is a fair description of leaders. It does not sort. Same-cohort test: it splits only accelerators (CBRS, -265.0 from -55.3). In memory WDC's margin rose from 26.4 to 43.6 and it lagged. In software the laggard APP's rose. In internet the leader META's fell from 43.0 to 34.8 while laggard RDDT's rose from 13.6 to 28.8. In servers the laggard SHAZ 'improved' from -900.7 to -624.8, which shows the measure means nothing for companies with almost no sales (SMR -85337.3, OKLO -17981.1). The laggards whose margins fell are again mostly miners and power names. Harder cut 10 of 10 against 5 of 14 passes on that same mix. I am marking this harshly: true of leaders, too common among laggards to be a test.

verdicts.condition: share count is up more than 3% in a year
verdicts.why: Leaders 6 of 25, laggards 16 of 22. Harder cut: 1 of 10 against 13 of 15. One reading. Of the laggards over the line, all but SHAZ, TTWO, WDC and CBRS are miners or power names, businesses that must sell stock to build. Same-cohort test: it splits accelerators clearly (CBRS 61.2 against AMD 1.1, MRVL 2.6, TSM 0.0) and memory weakly (WDC 6.7, but mid-field STX is 5.5). It fails in servers (leader SMCI is 11.0, over the line too), software (laggard APP -1.8) and internet (DKNG, BKNG and NFLX are shrinking their count and lagged). Leaders AXTI (40.1) and PANW (22.3) issued heavily and led. It is knowable ahead and not circular, and it does fit CBRS. But as counted here it mostly says 'is a capital-hungry builder'. The 3% line is arbitrary: leaders CRWD (3.2) and S (3.3) sit just over it.

Leaders 21 of 25, laggards 8 of 22, one reading. The small laggards are the miners and power names (WULF 7.5, CIFR 6.4, CORZ 5.4, SMR 3.5, EOSE 1.2). Same-cohort test: it splits only servers (SMCI 28.6, SHAZ 1.7). CBRS is worth 42.1 and lagged. WDC 153.9, APP 93.3, NFLX 286.1, BKNG 118.4 and IBM 208.5 are large and lagged. In software the laggard APP (93.3) is bigger than leaders TWLO (43.1) and NTNX (19.9). It is also partly circular, because size is measured after the run. ENTG is 25.4 now and was 19.8 on 15 Sep. SMCI is 28.6, was 23.4. TSEM is 29.2, was 22.1. Those clear the line only because they rose. Harder cut 8 of 10 against 4 of 15: same mix.

verdicts.condition: ROSE between 30 June and 15 September while the chip fund fell 17%
verdicts.why: This is the price move itself. Three-month return is one of the three scores that define a leader, and 30 Jun to 15 Sep is most of those three months. A stock that rose then is a leader partly because it rose then. It is also a sector label: the names that rose are mostly cyber, software and storage, and in that stretch the software fund gained 16.5 and the cyber fund 12.4 while the chip fund lost 17.3. It covers only 13 of 25 leaders; the chip leaders and DDOG fell and still lead. The one laggard that rose, NFLX, then rolled over. It cannot be tested on the harder cut, where by design everyone fell.

survivors: management RAISED its own guidance at the last report: the one real separator, and only between groups of companies, not between stocks inside a group
analysts RAISED the earnings estimate over the last 90 days: survives, but it is the same news as the guidance raise, so count it once

summary: One claim stands: the leaders were companies whose outlook was going up, with management raising its own forecast at 24 of 25 leaders against 3 of 20 laggards, and at 10 of 10 names that fell and bounced against 1 of 14 that fell and stayed down. The page must add that this sorted groups, not stocks inside a group: CBRS, WDC, RDDT, MU, SNDK and STX all raised and did not lead, META led without a raise, and the study read only 52 of the 145 names. Profit, cash generation, having a price-to-earnings figure, rising margins, share count and size mostly describe what kind of company the laggards are (miners turned data-centre landlords, nuclear and battery developers, a new listing), and APP, BKNG and RDDT pass every one of them and still lagged. 'Peers were up' and 'rose during the summer fall' are the price move said twice, the analyst earnings lines are the guidance news counted again, and the sales-estimate line has too few laggard readings (2 of 7) to state.
